fable-5.1.text:
Well, let me explain the mechanics of it, because I think of these things as cause-effect relationships that repeat over and over again throughout history. I've studied the last 500 years of the rises and declines of the major empires and their currencies, and there's a pattern. I call it the big cycle, and bubbles and political conflict are not separate things. They're different stages of the same cycle.

It starts with debt. When you have a period of peace and prosperity, people borrow, they invest, asset prices go up, and that works for a while because the borrowing is producing income that pays the debt back. But at some point, the debt grows faster than the income that's needed to service it. People start buying things not because they're worth it, but because the prices have been going up, and they extrapolate that. That's the bubble. Everybody's happy, everybody feels rich, and the wealth that's being created is mostly on paper.

Now here's the key thing. During that bubble phase, the gains don't go to everybody equally. They go to the people who own the assets. So you get a widening wealth gap at exactly the same time that you have a lot of debt. And then the bubble bursts, as it always does, because the debts can't be paid. And when it bursts, the central bank has to come in and print money and buy financial assets, which helps the people who own financial assets again, and it devalues the money of the people who don't.

So now you have a situation where a large part of the population feels the system isn't working for them. They're not wrong. And when people are in economic pain and there's a big wealth gap, that's when you get populism. You get the left populists and the right populists, and they both agree on one thing, which is that the system is rigged, and they stop agreeing on everything else. That's the internal conflict. You've seen it in the 1930s, you've seen it in the 1890s, you've seen it in the decline of the Dutch and the British.

And the internal conflict then feeds into the external conflict, because a country that's divided and in debt is a country that's weaker, and that's usually when a rising power is challenging the existing one. So the bubble, the bust, the wealth gap, the populism, the breakdown of order, those are all links in one chain. They're not six different problems. They're one cycle.

I'm not saying it's destiny. I'm saying that if you understand where you are in the cycle, you can see what's likely to come next, and you can prepare for it. Most people don't, because the last time it happened was before they were born, and they think it's unprecedented. It's not unprecedented. It's just unprecedented in their lifetime.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I look at it is mechanically, as cause-and-effect relationships. Everything that has happened before happens over and over again for basically the same reasons. When I studied the last 500 years, the rise and decline of the Dutch empire, the British empire, the United States, China's dynasties, I saw the same patterns repeating. I call that the big cycle.

There are five big forces that drive it: the debt and money cycle, the internal order and disorder cycle, the external order and disorder cycle between great powers, acts of nature like droughts, floods, and pandemics, and technology and human inventiveness. They're all interrelated.

So let's take the relationship you asked about, bubbles and conflict. In the debt cycle, when times are good, people borrow. Debt grows faster than the incomes needed to service it, and asset prices go up. People extrapolate the past. They think if they buy, they'll make money, so they borrow to buy, and that creates a bubble. Credit is spending power, and one person's debt is another person's asset. The more that goes on, the more wealth and the gaps in wealth grow, because the people who own the assets benefit and the people who don't get left behind.

Then the bubble reaches the point where it can't go on. The central bank tightens, or the debt service gets too heavy, and it bursts. Now you have bad economic times *and* a large wealth gap at the same time. Historically, that combination is the most reliable indicator that internal conflict is coming. When the pie is growing, people can fight over how it's divided and still get along. When it's shrinking and the gaps are big, people turn on each other.

That's when you get populism of the left and populism of the right. You get polarization, and people stop being willing to compromise. Each side believes it's right and that winning is more important than following the rules. That's a dangerous stage. In my template it's the stage just before a kind of civil war, and I don't necessarily mean a shooting war. I mean the rule of law breaks down and the system can no longer resolve disagreements.

At the same time, the central bank typically responds to the bust by printing money and buying debt, which devalues money. That's another part of the cycle. And if that's happening while a rising power is challenging the existing power, you get external conflict layered on top of the internal conflict. The 1930s are the classic example: a debt bubble in the 1920s, a bust in 1929, money printing, populism, wealth gaps, then the conflicts inside countries and between them.

So I would say the bubble isn't the cause of the conflict by itself. It's the debt dynamics, the wealth gaps they create, and then the pain when they reverse. Those are the conditions in which political conflict grows. And when I look at where we are now, with very high debt levels, big wealth and values gaps, and great-power rivalry, those conditions look very much like the ones that preceded difficult periods before. That's why I think it's so important that people understand how the machine works, so they can prepare for it rather than be surprised by it.

fable-5.text:
Well, if you look at history — and I studied the last 500 years, really the rises and declines of reserve currency empires, the Dutch, the British, the Americans — you see the same things happening over and over again, like a cycle. And bubbles and political conflict are not separate things. They're connected parts of the same machine.

Here's how it works. Bubbles happen because credit creates buying power. When you lend somebody money, they can spend more, and one person's spending is another person's income, so the whole thing feeds on itself and everybody feels richer. Asset prices go up, people borrow against those assets, and they extrapolate that the good times will continue. But debt is a promise to deliver money in the future, and when debts grow faster than the incomes needed to service them — which is what always happens in a bubble — you eventually hit the point where the debts can't be paid back. That's when the bubble bursts.

Now, here's where the politics comes in. During the bubble, the gains are not distributed evenly. Those who own assets — stocks, real estate — get much richer, and those who don't, don't. So you build up a large wealth gap at the same time you're building up the debt. Then when the bubble bursts, you have an economic downturn, and that downturn hits hardest the people who were already left behind. And when you have a big wealth gap together with a big economic downturn, history shows you get populism of the left and populism of the right, and you get internal conflict over how to divide a shrinking pie. People fight much more over a shrinking pie than a growing one.

And then the central bank responds the only way it can, which is to print money and buy debt. That's what happened in 1933, in 2008, in 2020. The printing of money devalues the currency and it pushes asset prices up again — which benefits asset holders — so it actually widens the wealth gap further, and that intensifies the political conflict. So you get this self-reinforcing dynamic: the bubble creates the gap, the bust creates the anger, and the remedy amplifies both.

The last time we saw this full configuration — a debt bubble bursting, big wealth gaps, internal populist conflict, and a rising great power challenging an existing one — was the 1930s. And we know how that period went. So when I look at where we are in the big cycle today, I don't look at the bubble as just a financial event. I look at it as the thing that sets the political conflict in motion. Financial crises don't just cost money — they change who people are angry at, and they change political orders. That's the relationship.

opus-5.text:
Well, let me explain how I came to see it, because I didn't start with a theory. I started with surprises.

In 2008, I was surprised. In 1971, when Nixon took us off the gold standard, I was surprised. And whenever something surprises me, it means it didn't happen in my lifetime, so I go back and study it in other periods and other countries. And when I did that — going back 500 years, through the Dutch, the British, the Chinese dynasties — I found that these things aren't mysterious at all. They're mechanical. The same cause-effect relationships repeat because human nature repeats.

So here's the mechanic. A bubble is just credit creating buying power that isn't backed by real productivity. When it bursts, you have a debt problem, and there are only a few ways to deal with debt: you default, you austerity, you redistribute wealth, or you print money. Politically, printing is always the path of least resistance. Nobody feels it immediately. But that printed money doesn't go evenly into the economy — it goes into financial assets. And who owns financial assets? The top ten percent. So the very medicine you use to cure the debt crisis widens the wealth gap.

Now you have a large population of people who are not participating, and they look across and see others doing fantastically well. That produces populism — and it's important to understand populism of the left and populism of the right are the same phenomenon. A populist is somebody who says: I will fight for you. Not negotiate, not compromise — fight. And when you get a populist of the left and a populist of the right simultaneously, and the middle hollows out, that's when you lose the thing that actually holds a system together, which is people's willingness to abide by a shared set of rules.

The test comes when there's a contested outcome — an election, a court decision — and one side says, I'm not accepting that. In my study of history, that's the moment the internal order breaks. Not the bubble bursting. The bubble is maybe step three of six.

And here's the part that worries me most: this internal conflict cycle tends to line up with the external one. A rising power challenging an existing power. Debt, internal disorder, great power conflict — they're not separate stories, they reinforce each other. That alignment is what I mean by the Big Cycle, and we are, in my opinion, quite late in it.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Let me describe the pattern, because I think it repeats across history. I've studied the last 500 years or so, and the same forces keep coming up.

There are a few big forces that drive change. The first is the money and credit cycle: debt and credit get created, they fuel spending and investment, and eventually you get bubbles. People borrow to buy assets that have been going up, and the rising prices make them feel richer and more confident, so they borrow more. Then the debt burdens become too large relative to the income that services them, and the bubble bursts. When that happens, central banks print money to ease the pain, which tends to help people who own assets more than people who don't.

That leads to the second force, which is the internal political and social cycle. In the good times, a lot of wealth gets created, but it usually gets distributed very unevenly. So you build up big gaps in wealth, in opportunity, and in values. Then a downturn comes. When the economy is good, people can tolerate those gaps. When it turns bad, they can't. The people who feel they're losing get angry and look for someone to blame, and you get populism on the left and the right, each with its own champion. Politics becomes more about fighting than about solving problems, and the two sides stop seeing each other as fellow citizens with a disagreement and start seeing each other as enemies. That's when the system of rules, the courts, the legislatures, and the norms, starts to break down, because people care more about winning than about the rules.

So bubbles and political conflict aren't separate things. The financial boom creates the conditions, meaning too much debt, big wealth gaps, and complacency. The bust then puts pressure on those conditions. Economic pain and political conflict feed each other, and in the extreme you get things like revolutions, civil conflict, or autocratic takeovers, because people want order and will give up a lot to get it.

The third force is the external order, the rise and decline of great powers. When a dominant country is financially strained and politically divided, it's more vulnerable to challenge from rising powers. Then you have trade wars, technology wars, capital wars, and sometimes military wars. And on top of all this are acts of nature, such as droughts, floods, and pandemics, which can speed things up or slow them down.

What I'm saying isn't that it's pre-determined. It's that these are cause-and-effect relationships that play out over and over, and if you understand them you can see where we are in the cycle and act accordingly. By my read, we're in a stage where debts are very large, the wealth and values gaps are big, the politics is highly polarized, and the world order is being challenged. That combination is what I think deserves serious attention.

haiku-5.5.text:
Yes. I think of bubbles as a debt story first. Debt is a promise that the future will be bigger than the past. When credit grows faster than incomes for long enough, asset prices rise, people feel richer, and whoever already owns assets pulls far ahead. Eventually the cash flows can't cover the promises, and the bust comes with deleveraging and defaults. Central banks cut rates and create more money to cushion it, which keeps the system going but widens the gap further.

The political part comes from what that does to distribution. During the expansion, the gains go mostly to people with capital. Many others feel left behind, even when their lives are materially better than before. In the bust, the pain lands on people who didn't create the bubble, and the institutions meant to protect them often look like they're protecting the people who did. That gap between those who own and those who don't, and between what people were told and what they experience, is where populism comes from. You see distrust of experts and central banks, and a pull toward leaders who promise to fix things by force of will.

In the big cycle, the internal conflict doesn't stay internal. When it gets severe enough, the government's ability to make and carry out decisions weakens. At the same time, a rising power often challenges the existing order from outside. So the debt cycle feeds internal conflict, and internal conflict makes a country more vulnerable externally. That shows up as trade wars, sanctions, and sometimes war.

The 1930s is the example I'd point to. There was a debt and bubble problem, a severe deleveraging, deep political polarization, and then a very dangerous geopolitical outcome. History doesn't repeat exactly. But the sequence of debt, distribution, and conflict is worth watching, because that's usually where the warning signs appear first.

astra-6.text:
Well, they’re connected. You can’t really understand the financial cycle without understanding how it affects people and how those people behave politically.

Think about what happens when you create a lot of debt. Somebody borrows money, they spend it, and that spending becomes somebody else’s income. That’s good on the way up. Credit expands, asset prices rise, and people feel richer. And rising prices encourage more borrowing, so that process can reinforce itself.

But the debt is a claim on future money. Eventually, you reach a point where the debt payments are growing faster than the incomes needed to service them. Then you have a problem: who’s going to bear the losses?

That’s where the financial issue becomes a political issue. Those who own assets may have done very well during the boom, while other people feel they haven’t participated. When the downturn comes, those differences become much harder to manage. People argue over bailouts, taxes, spending cuts, and the creation of money. They lose confidence in institutions, and they become more attracted to leaders who promise to fight for their side.

And that can happen at the same time that countries are competing over wealth and power. Internal conflict can weaken a country, while external competition puts additional pressure on it.

So when I talk about the big cycle, I’m looking at the interaction of debt and money, internal political order, and the international order. A bubble doesn’t automatically produce a conflict. But when financial stress meets large wealth gaps and an inability to compromise, the risks reinforce one another. The important question is whether people can deal with those adjustments together.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the way to understand it is that the financial system and the political system are connected through who gets wealth, who gets opportunity, and who bears the losses when things go wrong.

In a boom, credit expands. People borrow money to buy assets, those assets rise in price, and that makes people feel wealthier and able to borrow more. But those debts are claims on future income. If the claims grow faster than the income available to service them, you build up a vulnerability.

When that reverses, it becomes a political question: Who’s going to pay? Will you let borrowers fail? Will you tax people? Cut spending? Create money? Each choice distributes the pain differently.

And if you already have large wealth gaps and people feel the system is unfair, that financial stress feeds conflict. People become more attracted to leaders who promise to fight for their side. Compromise becomes harder, and disagreements about economic policy become struggles over the rules of the system itself.

That’s part of what I mean by the big cycle: the debt and money cycle interacting with the cycle of internal political order, and also with the changing balance of power between countries. Domestic weakness can make international rivalry more dangerous, while international conflict puts more pressure on government finances.

These things reinforce one another. So when I look at a bubble, I’m also asking: How much financial capacity is there to absorb a loss, and how much trust is there to agree on how to share it?

luna-5.6.text:
I see them as parts of the same cycle. When debt builds up and money is easy, asset prices rise faster than incomes and productivity, so you get widening gaps between the rich and the poor. Eventually the debt can’t be serviced in the normal way, and the system has to choose between defaults, austerity, or creating money. That process redistributes wealth and creates resentment—especially when people feel the system is rigged.

At the same time, a rising power challenges the existing power, which increases geopolitical tension. So financial stress inside a country and rivalry between countries reinforce each other. History shows that when wealth gaps are large, politics becomes more populist and less willing to compromise, and when external conflict rises, it can deepen internal division. The big cycle is essentially the interaction of money, debt, internal conflict, and international conflict—and if those pressures aren’t managed well, they can lead to major changes in the domestic and global order.

I see them as connected parts of the same cycle. When credit is easy, asset prices rise and people feel prosperous, but the gains are often uneven. Debt builds up, and eventually the bubble turns: incomes and asset values fall, while debts remain. That squeeze tends to widen the gap between people who have a lot and people who have little, and it weakens trust in institutions. Then politics becomes more polarized, because people disagree not only about what to do, but about who should bear the losses.

At the same time, a country that’s heavily indebted may create money or restructure its debts, which can weaken confidence in its currency and its standing abroad. If its power is also being challenged by a rising competitor, economic stress can feed into geopolitical tension. None of that makes conflict inevitable. But in the big cycle, financial strain, internal division, and rivalry between countries can reinforce one another, so you have to look at them together.
